He Morphing has been implemented in CCWorldWeatherGen [8], WeatherShift [9], epwshiftr [10], and the Future Weather Genera- tor [11], and has become the de facto standard in building performance research. Recent community efforts through the IEA EBC Annex 80 pro- gramme [12,13] have produced pre-computed morphed weather files for representative cities, further embedding this workflow in practice. However, as Zeng et al. [14] noted in a comprehensive review, many existing approaches are primarily based on monthly or seasonal climate change signals, which may fail to capture sub-monthly variability that is important for accurately estimating peak loads. For energy systems planning, these morphed weather files underpin critical infrastructure decisions. National and regional energy agencies use building energy projections to assess generation adequacy, size reserve margins, and plan transmission capacity. Renewable energy integration studies rely on correlated building load and solar/wind generation profiles under future climates. Urban energy planners use morphed weather files to size district heating/cooling systems and forecast peak demand for grid reinforcement. Yet the systematic biases introduced by morphing workflows — and their specific origins — remain unquantified. If TMY baseline selection or monthly delta reso- lution systematically distorts heating vs. cooling demand, or suppresses extreme heat wave events that drive peak electricity loads, energy infrastructure sized using these files will be maladapted to the climate that actually materializes. Alternatives to morphing exist along a spectrum of complexity. Stochastic weather generators (SWGs) synthesize hourly sequences from statistical models trained on observations; Eames et al. [15] showed that UKCP09-based stochastic weather produces more real- istic future projections than morphing for UK locations. Dynamical downscaling uses RCM output directly to construct Future-TMY (F- ‘TMY) files, bypassing the morphing step entirely; comparative studies by Bravo Dias et al. [16] and Tootkaboni et al. [17] found mean- ingful discrepancies between morphed and dynamically downscaled weather files. Moazami et al. [18] demonstrated that morphing-based approaches struggle to capture changes in extreme event frequency and persistence. Reviews by Herrera et al. [19] and Zeng et al. [14] provide comprehensive taxonomies of these methods. Yet these comparative studies share a structural limitation: they compare complete methods against each other (morphing vs. stochastic generator vs. F-TMY), making it impossible to attribute performance differences to any single design choice. If a stochastic generator outper- forms morphing, is it because the generator uses observations instead of ‘TMY? Because it resolves daily variability? Or because it adds stochastic fluctuations? Without factorial isolation, the answer is unclear. A body of work in climate science provides the theoretical basis for expecting that monthly aggregation of climate change signals will suppress extreme events. Katz and Brown [20] demonstrated mathe- matically that extreme event frequencies depend more on changes in variability than on changes in the mean—implying that any method modifying only the mean (as monthly morphing does) will systemat- ically underestimate changes in extremes. Schir et al. [21] showed that the 2003 European heatwave cannot be explained by a mean shift alone; it required an increase in temperature variability, a signal invisible at monthly resolution. Fischer and Knutti [22] found that the anthropogenic signal is largest for the most extreme daily events— precisely the events erased by monthly averaging. More broadly, Ma- raun [23] showed in a critical review of bias correction methods that the delta/change-factor approach cannot add missing sub-monthly variability and will produce artifacts when applied to hourly data. For building energy simulation, this literature implies a clear pre- diction: monthly climate deltas will preserve the long-term trend but erase the day-to-day transitions that drive peak loads, thermal whiplash events, and equipment stress. This prediction has not been systemati- cally tested in the building energy context. Prior studies in building science have identified that errors exist in ‘TMY-morphed weather files [24-27] but have not isolated where they originate. Are the dominant errors caused by the TMY baseline, by monthly delta resolution, or by the absence of stochastic variability? ‘The answer has direct practical implications: if the baseline domi- nates, replacing TMY with observations is a low-cost fix; if monthly smoothing dominates, daily deltas are essential; if stochastic genera- tion is required, computationally intensive weather generators become necessary. We evaluate four weather generation methods against a recon- structed climate reference (RECON) over 2025-2100, using New York as the primary case study and Los Angeles as a secondary compar- ison, under weather projections derived from the CORDEX CMIPS RCP8.5 scenario, with generalizability assessed across six climate sce- narios. A factorial experimental design (detailed in Section 2.1) isolates three independent factors: baseline source, climate delta resolution, and stochastic generation. Specifically, we ask which routine workflow decisions — baseline file selection, climate delta temporal resolution — propagate the largest biases into degree-day estimates, peak loads, and extreme event representation, posing concrete risks to capacity planning and resilience assessment. ‘The contributions of this paper are: 1. A factorial experimental design that isolates three independent sources of error in climate-adapted weather files for the first time. 2. Quantification of the TMY3 baseline bias relative to a deter- ministic reference signal: +177 °C - days HDD and —74 °C- days CDD at New York, with the bias reversing sign at Los Angeles, demonstrating station-specific rather than correctable systematic error. 3. Demonstration — grounded in climate science theory and con- firmed empirically — that monthly-delta methods severely dis- tort extreme event representation: the ISD climatological base- line combined with a monthly delta eliminates within-month variability entirely, while TMY3+Monthly produces zero ther- mal whiplash events over 76 years. This finding is validated against an independent HVAC changeover metric (Supplemen- tary Figure $1), confirming that TMY3 systematically underrep- resents temperature transition extremes by design. 4. Evidence that stochastic weather generation contributes only 0.25°C RMSE relative to the deterministic reference, with its primary value lying in realistic inter-annual variability for en- semble and extreme-event applications. 2. Data and study domain The primary study site is New York JFK Airport (USAF 744860), with Los Angeles LAX (USAF 722950) as a secondary site for geographic generalizability. Hourly observations are drawn from the NOAA Integrated Surface Database (ISD) [31,32]. The training period is 1991-2010, provid- ing both the climatological baseline yysp and RS-VAR training data; the independent validation period 2011-2020 provides ground truth. Variables include dry-bulb temperature, dewpoint temperature, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure. Solar radiation (GHI, DNI, DHI) is obtained from the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) [33]. Real meteorological observations serve as the foundation for the entire factorial comparison: the ISD-derived climatology anchors three of the four methods and the RECON reference, while the independent 2011-2020 validation period provides ground-truth confirmation that the learned structures are physically realistic. The reliability of the downstream findings depends directly on the quality and completeness of these observational records. The TMY3 file for JFK (USA_NY_New. York-J.F.Kennedy . Intl. AP.744860_TMY3 . epw), generated by NREL from 1991-2005 NSRDB data [6], serves as the baseline for TMY3+Monthly, TMY3 is H. Guo and K. He selected because it remains the most widely used weather file format in building energy simulation practice: it is the default EPW format distributed with EnergyPlus, it underpins most morphing workflows in the literature, and it represents the standard against which practitioners currently make design decisions. The purpose of this study is to evalu- ate whether that standard introduces systematic biases—making TMY3 the natural baseline to test. Note the five-year discrepancy between the TMY3 source period (1991-2005) and the ISD baseline (1991- 2010). A sensitivity check confirms this is not a confound: the TMY3 mean temperature is 0.52°C below the 1991-2005 ISD mean (its own source period), versus 0.67 °C below the 1991-2010 mean. The baseline period shift accounts for only 0.15 °C; the remaining 0.52°C cool bias is intrinsic to the Finkelstein-Schafer month-selection algorithm. Climate change signals are derived from Coordinated Regional Cli- mate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX) regional climate projections driven by CMIPS [29,30]. The CORDEX provides dynamically down- scaled simulations by nesting RCMs within GCM outputs from CMIP. In this study, we use the REMO2015 RCM simulation, driven by bound- ary conditions from the MPI-ESM-LR GCM, within the North Amer- ican NAM-22 domain (~ 22 km resolution) under the RCP8.5 sce- nario. Five additional projection sources are tested for generalizability (Section 3.5). The analysis spans 2025-2100 (665,737 common hours across all methods, after excluding hours with missing data in any method and removing leap days—23 h fewer than the nominal 76 x 8760 = 665, 760 due to residual missingness alignment). All generated EPW files use a consistent 8760-hour non-leap-year calendar; leap days are omitted to maintain alignment with the standard EPW format, and the same omission policy is applied uniformly to all methods and the RECON reference. Period-averaged results use four sub-periods: 2025-2040, 2041-2060, 2061-2080, and 2081-2100. 2.4, Evaluation We conduct evaluation across two periods: 2011-2020 as an inde- pendent validation period to assess each method’s structural preserva- tion against ISD observations, and 2025-2100 as the future projection period to evaluate deviation from the historical extrapolation reference (RECON). Three aspects of weather file quality are evaluated: mean energy demand fidelity, extreme event preservation, and multivariate structure. These correspond, respectively, to a building’s annual energy budget, its peak load and resilience requirements, and the coupled physics of simultaneous thermal-solar-wind conditions. 2.4.1. Extreme events Four metrics test whether each method preserves realistic weather stress patterns: 1. Day-to-day temperature swings: the probability P(|T() — T(t—24) > 8°C) computed on hourly data, where T(1)—T(t—24) is the 24-hour temperature difference. This measures the frequency of large thermal transitions that drive peak loads. 2. Cold spell frequency: the count and duration of consecutive day sequences with T, < 0°C. Unrealistic cold spells (e.g., 30- day frozen periods) indicate temporal smoothing artifacts. 3. Thermal whiplash: a day with daily mean temperature >20°C followed by a >8°C drop in daily mean temperature to the subsequent day. These events force rapid HVAC mode- switching from cooling to heating demand. Supplementary Fig- ure S1 validates this metric using an alternative definition (HVAC changeover: heating++cooling transitions at 15/18 °C), confirm- ing the finding is not metric-dependent. 4. Rapid warming ramps: a >10°C rise in daily mean tempera- ture within 2 consecutive days. These events challenge cooling system capacity. These metrics are not intended as prescriptive definitions of building-relevant extreme events (which would depend on building type, occupancy, and local standards). Rather, they serve as diag- nostic probes chosen specifically for their sensitivity to the temporal resolution and baseline effects under study: they discriminate sharply between methods that preserve day-to-day variability and methods that smooth it. The specific thresholds (8°C swing, 0°C cold spell, 20°C/8°C whiplash, 10°C ramp) are practical choices sized to capture synoptic- scale transitions relevant to HVAC operation; the method ranking is insensitive to reasonable threshold variations (e.g., swing thresholds of 6°C or 10°C produce the same ordering). Supplementary Figure $1 validates the thermal whiplash finding against an independent HVAC changeover metric, confirming that the conclusion is not an artifact of any particular threshold definition. 2.4.3. Factor 1: Systematic energy demand bias from TMY3 baseline The most consequential finding of this study concerns the base- line source effect. Comparing TMY3+Monthly against ISD+Monthly — which differ only in their baseline (TMY3 composite vs. ISD climatol- ogy) while sharing the same monthly climate delta and deterministic morphing — reveals a large, systematic bias in energy demand metrics. Over 2025-2100, the TMY3-based method (TMY3+Monthly) pro- duces: + HDD bias: +177 °C - days relative to RECON (9% overestimate) + CDD bias: —74 °C - days relative to RECON (7% underestimate) In contrast, the observation-based ISD+Monthly method produces biases of only —53 °C - days for both HDD and CDD—a modest residual attributable to the nonlinear interaction between monthly smoothing and the degree-day threshold. The root cause of the TMY3 bias is the file’s systematic 0.7°C cool bias relative to actual observations—a consequence of the TMY selection algorithms preference for “typical” (ie., moderate) months. ‘Table 2 presents the HDD and CDD values by sub-period. The TMY3 baseline bias is remarkably stable across all time horizons, confirming that it is a structural property of the TMY composite rather than a feature of any particular climate period. Fig. 3 shows the HDD/CDD trajectories from 1973 to 2100, span- ning the historical validation period (2011-2020) and the forecast period (2025-2100). The upper panels present 10-year rolling means. ‘TMY3+Monthly exhibits a persistent systematic offset—overestimating HDD by about +205 °C - days (2030-2060) and underestimating CDD by approximately —46 °C - days. In contrast, ISD-based methods and sAMY closely track RECON throughout the projection. The lower panels show annual values.
